Key audit matter:
The main portion of impairment for loans and
advances to the customers is individually calculated
as the difference between the carrying amount and
the present value of estimated future cash flows
discounted at the original effective interest rate of
the loan. The key judgment applied is on the value of
collateral charged to the Group and the Bank and the
estimated period of recovery.
Where no objective evidence of impairment exists
for an individually assessed loans and advances, the
balance is included in a group of loans and advances
with similar credit risk characteristics and collectively
assessed for impairment using an unidentified
impairment model.
The unidentified impairment model is based on
empirical data on ‘loss’ ratios over the past three
years. Management apply judgment based on their
current experiences/knowledge of the current loan
book to adjust the unidentified impairment amount
as determined by the model.
This is a significant area of judgment. The significant
judgements and areas of uncertainty embodied in
the impairment assessment are disclosed in Note 3
of the financial statements.
How our audit addressed the Key audit ma:
For individually calculated impairment, we tested a sample of
loans and advances to ascertain whether the loss event (that is
the point at which impairment is recognised) had been identified
in a timely manner including, where relevant, how forbearance
had been considered. This was done by reviewing the performance
of borrowers. Impairment assessment was driven by cash flows,
we tested the completeness and accuracy of the key inputs.
Where impairment had been identified, and an impairment
assessment was driven by cash flows, we tested the completeness
and accuracy of the key inputs such as repayment history and
discount rates and recomputed the cash flows.
We agreed the forced sale values to collateral valuation reports
for physical assets, where an impairment assessment was driven
by recovery of collateral. We then reviewed the reasonableness
of discount rates and recovery period used in determining the
recoverable amounts of collateral. In the case of collectively
assessed impairment, we tested reasonableness of the loss
ratio by validating historical data used by management and
reasonableness of adjustments made to the historical loss ratios
to reflect current risk in the portfolio.

Key audit matter:
Revenue recognition dependent on IT systems
The Bank’s financial accounting and reporting
systems are heavily dependent on complex systems.
Specifically, the computation and recognition of
income on loans and advances, forex income and
other trading income is largely dependent on the IT
systems of the Bank.
Significant reliance on IT systems presents a
significant risk to the bank as the core banking
system is considered complex due to the multiple
significant functionalities and interdependence with
other systems.
The possible financial implications of errors or
frauds on the financial statements, either directly or
indirectly will usually be significant.
There is a risk that automated accounting procedures
and related IT dependent manual controls are not
designed and operating effectively.
How our audit addressed the Key audit ma:
We assessed and tested the design and operating effectiveness of
the controls over the continued integrity of the IT systems that
are relevant to the revenue cycle and financial accounting and
reporting in general.
We examined the framework of governance over the Group’s IT
organisation and the controls over program development and
changes, access to programs and data and IT operations, including
compensating controls where required. Where necessary we also
carried out direct tests of certain aspects of the security of the
Group’s IT systems including access management and segregation
of duties.
We performed tests on the core banking system and other
significant systems to satisfy ourselves of the integrity on the
processing of financial information and confirm appropriate
implementation of IT security controls.
We tested the Information Technology General Controls (ITGCs)
and application controls for “Flexcube 12” around computation
of interest income and fees and commission to ensure that
applications are working accurately and as designed. We also
tested interfaces of other systems with “Flexcube 12” to ensure
completeness of data flow.
In addition to the work done on the systems, we performed
appropriate analytical reviews on the interest income and fees
and commissions lines as well as testing manual journals posted
to the revenue lines.
